items.note: Inscription of Vikram Samvat 1229 names Lunapasaka as provincial governor of Udaipur in 1171 CE in the Bhailasvami Mahadvadashaka province.
Udayaditya took refuge with Bhailasvami for removal of poverty; an inscription relating to it was found at Bijamandal (also lists grants of Yashovarman and Lakshmivarman).
Ancient name of Bhailasvamipur was Vidisha; mentions in Ramayana, Puranas, Jataka and Jain literature; Malavikagnimitra set in Vidisha, the Shunga capital.
878 CE Mahalghat inscription: two bazaars of Bhailasvami let out on rent, 130 panchiyaka dramma donated to the Sun temple.
Udaipur is listed with Dhar, Ujjayini and Gyaraspur as places with excellent examples of Paramara art, like Mandu.
Pratapgarh inscription of 946 CE, Someshvara's defeat of Bhoj in 1046 CE, and Bhoj's forts of Dhar and Mandu.
Only Dhara received a distinctive Paramara-era literary description; Bhoj conceived the ideal town in the Samarangana-sutradhara and gave it concrete form as Dhara.
Because of Bhoj's dam, Vidisha no longer faced the Betwa's flood danger; Bhoj founded Bhailasvamidevapura on land lower than the Betwa water-area, later Bhelsa.
Near Bhojpur, by damming the Betwa, Bhoj built a lake.
Paramara-era bastions were square; examples at Dhar, Vidisha and Omkareshvara forts.
Paramara-era rampart gates were swastika-shaped rather than straight, found at Dhar, Burhi Mandav, Omkareshvara, Vidisha.
Paramara towns described as temple-dominated; each had one chief shrine, at Vidisha the Sun temple of Bhailasvami.
Paramara-era towns protected by moat, rampart and river or tanks; Dhara, Mandav, Omkareshvara, Vidisha and Modi examples.
Neighbouring kings probably laid out towns similarly; architectural currents had mutual influence and treatises were common.

items.note: Prescribed placement of the four varnas in a town, with merchants, physicians and army in all four directions.
Outside the town a shrine in the east and a cremation-ground in the south.
Arthashastra rules on brahmadeya grants of land to priests and teachers, free of fine and tax.
Commercial towns to be founded for import, export and trade at mineral centres and on merchant-routes.
Prescriptions for the rampart on the vapra or dhulakota: brick proportions, height 12 to 24 cubits, broad top, coping; no wooden rampart.
Gate prescriptions: door-leaves, bolts, pivot-pin, chief door broad enough for four elephants.
A stepwell (vapi) to be built in the middle of the rampart.
Prescribed settlement of weavers, wool-workers, leather and bamboo craftsmen, shops, hospitals, and guilds and foreign traders.
Temples of Shiva, Shri and others in the middle of the town; shrines and holy places outside the moat.
Prescription for a slab-built stepwell treasury; the Champa stepwell of Mandav cited as a beautiful example.
Varahamihira's Brihat-samhita dimensions for royal houses (135x108 cubits finest, down to 95x76) as general domestic-architecture background.
